sections.title: Section A · Textbook-style questions
sections.note: Like the "Figure it Out" questions in NCERT Ganita Prakash.

questions.text: Which of these expressions are even for every whole number $n$?
steps: An expression is "always even" only if it is even for every $n$. So we try to write it as $2\times(\text{something})$, or we find one value of $n$ that makes it odd.
(a) $4n+2=2(2n+1)$. It has the factor $2$, so it is always even.
(b) $n^2+n=n(n+1)$. Of two numbers next to each other, one is even. So the product is always even.
(c) $3n+1$: for $n=2$ it is $7$, which is odd. So it is not always even.
(d) $(n+1)(n+2)$ is again a product of two numbers next to each other. So it is always even.
(e) $5n$: for $n=1$ it is $5$, which is odd. So it is not always even.

questions.text: Put $+$ or $-$ signs between $11, 12, 13, 14$ in all possible ways. Show that you never get an odd answer.
steps: First take all $+$ signs: $11+12+13+14=50$. This is even.
Now change one sign, for example $+13$ to $-13$. The answer goes down by $13+13=26$, that is, by $2\times13$.
In general, changing $+x$ to $-x$ changes the answer by $2x$. A change of $2x$ is even, so an even answer stays even.
Each other choice of signs comes from $50$ by such changes. Example: $11-12+13-14=-2$, which is even.

questions.text: Find the remainder when $1{,}234{,}567$ is divided by each number. Do not divide.
steps: (a) For $2$, look only at the last digit. $7$ is odd, so the remainder is $1$.
(b) For $4$, look only at the last two digits: $67=4\times16+3$. The remainder is $3$.
(c) For $8$, look only at the last three digits: $567=8\times70+7$. The remainder is $7$.
(d) For $9$, add the digits: $1+2+3+4+5+6+7=28$. Then $28=9\times3+1$. The remainder is $1$.

questions.text: Without dividing, check whether $3{,}87{,}234$ is divisible by $2$, $3$, $4$, $6$, $8$, $9$ and $11$.
steps: By $2$: the last digit is $4$, which is even. Yes.
By $3$ and $9$: digit sum $=3+8+7+2+3+4=27$. $27$ is a multiple of $3$ and of $9$. Yes to both.
By $6$: the number is divisible by $2$ and by $3$, and $2$ and $3$ have no common factor. Yes.
By $4$: the last two digits are $34$, and $34=4\times8+2$. No. So it is not divisible by $8$ either, because every multiple of $8$ is a multiple of $4$.
By $11$: from the right, odd places $4+2+8=14$, even places $3+7+3=13$. $14-13=1$, not $0$. No.
questions.answer: Divisible by $2$, $3$, $6$ and $9$; not by $4$, $8$ or $11$.

questions.text: Find all the digits $x$ for which $43x2$ is divisible by $3$. Then find the digits for which it is divisible by $9$.
steps: Digit sum $=4+3+x+2=9+x$.
For $3$: $9+x$ must be a multiple of $3$. Since $9$ is already a multiple of $3$, $x$ must be a multiple of $3$: $x=0, 3, 6, 9$.
For $9$: $9+x$ must be $9$ or $18$. So $x=0$ or $x=9$.

questions.text: Find the digit $x$ so that $9{,}x82$ is divisible by $11$.
steps: Number the places from the right: $2$ (1st), $8$ (2nd), $x$ (3rd), $9$ (4th).
Odd places: $2+x$. Even places: $8+9=17$.
Difference: $(2+x)-17=x-15$. It must be $0$ or a multiple of $11$.
$x$ is a digit from $0$ to $9$, so $x-15$ is between $-15$ and $-6$. The only multiple of $11$ there is $-11$. So $x-15=-11$ and $x=4$.
Check: $9482=11\times862$.

questions.text: Write the general form of a three-digit number with digits $a, b, c$. Then write the general form of the number with the digits in reverse order.
steps: In the number $abc$, the digit $a$ is in the hundreds place, $b$ in the tens place and $c$ in the units place.
So the number is $100a+10b+c$.
The reversed number has $c$ in the hundreds place and $a$ in the units place: $100c+10b+a$.

questions.text: Find the digital root of $8{,}74{,}352$. What is the remainder when this number is divided by $9$?
steps: Add the digits: $8+7+4+3+5+2=29$.
Add again: $2+9=11$. Again: $1+1=2$.
The digital root is not $9$, so it is also the remainder on division by $9$.

questions.text: A hall has $38$ chairs. They are arranged in rows of $6$. How many full rows are there, and how many chairs are left over? Write $38$ in the form $6k+r$.
steps: Count in sixes: $6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36$. That is $6$ full rows.
$38-36=2$ chairs are left over.
So $38=6\times6+2$. The remainder $2$ is less than $6$, as it must be.

items.v: How many rows? How many left?

questions.text: Draw a Venn diagram for the multiples of $4$, $8$ and $32$. Is there a number that is a multiple of $32$ but not of $4$?
steps: $32=8\times4$, so every multiple of $32$ is a multiple of $8$: $32k=8(4k)$.
$8=4\times2$, so every multiple of $8$ is a multiple of $4$: $8k=4(2k)$.
So the circle for $32$ is inside the circle for $8$, which is inside the circle for $4$.
questions.answer: No such number. The circles sit one inside the other.

answerPicture.caption: Every multiple of 32 is a multiple of 8, and every multiple of 8 is a multiple of 4.

sections.title: Section B · Reference-book style (as in RS Aggarwal)
sections.note: General form of numbers, reversal and missing digits.

questions.text: The sum of a two-digit number and the number with its digits reversed is $143$. The units digit is $5$ more than the tens digit. Find the number.
steps: Let the tens digit be $a$ and the units digit be $b$. The number is $10a+b$; the reversed number is $10b+a$.
Also $b=a+5$. Put this in: $a+a+5=13$, so $2a=8$ and $a=4$. Then $b=9$.

questions.text: The difference of a two-digit number and its reversal is $54$. Find the difference of its digits. Give two such numbers.
steps: Pairs of digits with difference $6$: $(7,1)$, $(8,2)$, $(9,3)$, $(6,0)$.
Check one: $71-17=54$.

questions.text: $21y5$ is a multiple of $9$, where $y$ is a digit. Find $y$.
steps: Digit sum $=2+1+y+5=8+y$.
It must be a multiple of $9$. Since $8\le8+y\le17$, the only choice is $8+y=9$.
So $y=1$. Check: $2115=9\times235$.

questions.text: $31z5$ is a multiple of $3$, where $z$ is a digit. Find all possible values of $z$.
steps: Digit sum $=3+1+z+5=9+z$.
$9$ is a multiple of $3$, so $9+z$ is a multiple of $3$ exactly when $z$ is.
The digits that are multiples of $3$ are $0, 3, 6, 9$.

questions.text: A three-digit number has digits $a, b, c$ (in that order). Show that the number minus its reversal is divisible by $99$. What is the quotient?
steps: The number is $100a+10b+c$. Its reversal is $100c+10b+a$.
Subtract: $100a+10b+c-100c-10b-a$.
The $10b$ terms cancel: $99a-99c=99(a-c)$.
So the difference is $99$ times $(a-c)$.

questions.text: Find the digits $A$ and $B$: $\begin{array}{r}3A\\+\,25\\\hline B2\end{array}$
steps: Units column: $A+5$ ends in $2$. The only digit that works is $A=7$, because $7+5=12$. Write $2$ and carry $1$.
Tens column: $3+2+1$ (the carry) $=6$. So $B=6$.

questions.text: Prove that the product of any three consecutive numbers is divisible by $6$.
steps: Among two consecutive numbers, one is even. So among three, at least one is even: the product is divisible by $2$.
Among three consecutive numbers, exactly one is a multiple of $3$ (the remainders on division by $3$ are $0$, $1$, $2$ in some order). So the product is divisible by $3$.
$2$ and $3$ have no common factor, so a number divisible by both is divisible by $2\times3=6$.
Example: $4\times5\times6=120=6\times20$.

questions.text: Show that $n^3-n$ is divisible by $6$ for every whole number $n$.
steps: Take out the common factor: $n^3-n=n(n^2-1)$.
This is a product of three consecutive numbers, so by the last question it is divisible by $6$.

questions.text: Find the smallest number that leaves remainders $1, 2, 3$ and $4$ when it is divided by $2, 3, 4$ and $5$.
steps: In each case the remainder is $1$ less than the divisor. So if we add $1$ to the number, every remainder becomes $0$.
So the number $+1$ is a common multiple of $2, 3, 4, 5$.
The smallest common multiple (LCM) of $2, 3, 4, 5$ is $60$.
So the number is $60-1=59$. Check: $59=2\times29+1=3\times19+2=4\times14+3=5\times11+4$.

questions.text: $N$ leaves remainder $5$ on division by $8$. Find the remainder when $3N+7$ is divided by $8$.
steps: Write $N=8k+5$.
$24k$ is a multiple of $8$, and $22=8\times2+6$.
Shortcut: use only the remainder. $3\times5+7=22$, which leaves $6$.

questions.text: Can you write $100$ as the sum of $11$ odd numbers? Explain.
steps: Two odd numbers add to an even number. So $10$ odd numbers (five pairs) add to an even number.
Even $+$ the eleventh odd number $=$ odd.
So the sum of $11$ odd numbers is always odd. But $100$ is even.

questions.text: Without calculating, is $2^{10}+3^{10}$ even or odd? Is $2^{10}\times3^{10}$ a multiple of $4$?
steps: $2^{10}=2\times2\times\dots\times2$ is even.
$3^{10}$ is a product of odd numbers, so it is odd.
Even $+$ odd $=$ odd, so $2^{10}+3^{10}$ is odd.
$2^{10}\times3^{10}$ has at least two factors of $2$ ($2\times2=4$), so it is a multiple of $4$.
questions.answer: The sum is odd; the product is a multiple of $4$.

sections.title: Section D · Case studies
sections.note: Read the situation and answer each part.

questions.text: Case study: A school has $1{,}236$ students for a sports day.
steps: (a) Teams of $6$: $6=2\times3$. $1236$ is even, and its digit sum $1+2+3+6=12$ is a multiple of $3$. So yes: $1236\div6=206$ teams.
(b) Groups of $4$: the last two digits are $36=4\times9$. So yes: $1236\div4=309$ groups.
(c) Groups of $8$: the last three digits are $236=8\times29+4$. So no; $4$ students are left.
(d) Lines of $9$: digit sum $12=9+3$, so $3$ students are left. $9-3=6$ more students make full lines: $1242=9\times138$.
questions.answer: (a) Yes, $206$ teams (b) Yes, $309$ groups (c) No, $4$ left (d) $3$ left; $6$ more needed
parts: (a) Can the students be divided exactly into teams of $6$?
(b) Can they be divided exactly into groups of $4$?
(c) Into groups of $8$? If not, how many students are left?
(d) How many students are left when they make lines of $9$? How many more students are needed to make full lines?

questions.text: Case study: Ravi chooses a $3\times3$ square of dates on a calendar.
steps: (a) In a calendar, the date below is $7$ more, and the date to the right is $1$ more. With middle date $n$, the nine dates are $n-8, n-7, n-6, n-1, n, n+1, n+6, n+7, n+8$.
The $-8$ and $+8$ cancel, and so do $-7$ and $+7$, $-6$ and $+6$, $-1$ and $+1$. The sum is $9n$.
(b) The sum is $9\times n$, so it is always a multiple of $9$.
(d) $9n=216$, so $n=24$. The smallest date is the top-left one: $24-8=16$.
questions.answer: (a) sum $=9n$ (b) it is $9$ times the middle date (c) $17$ (d) $16$
parts: (a) If the middle date is $n$, write all nine dates and their sum.
(b) Explain why the sum is always a multiple of $9$.
(c) The sum is $153$. Find the middle date.
(d) The sum is $216$. Find the smallest date in the square.

sections.title: Section E · Assertion and reason
sections.note: Decide whether each statement is true, and whether the reason explains the assertion.

questions.text: Assertion (A): $7{,}344$ is divisible by $24$. Reason (R): $7{,}344$ is divisible by $3$ and by $8$, and $3$ and $8$ have no common factor.
steps: Check A: $7344\div24=306$. A is true.
Check R: last three digits $344=8\times43$, so it is divisible by $8$. Digit sum $=18$, so it is divisible by $3$. R is true.
Does R explain A? Yes: $24=3\times8$ with no common factor, so divisibility by $3$ and $8$ gives divisibility by $24$.
options: (i) Both A and R are true, and R explains A.
(ii) Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A.
(iii) A is true, but R is false.
(iv) A is false, but R is true.

questions.text: Assertion (A): The sum of four consecutive numbers is a multiple of $4$. Reason (R): The sum of four consecutive numbers is $4n+6$.
steps: Check R: $n+(n+1)+(n+2)+(n+3)=4n+6$. R is true.
Check A: $4n+6=4(n+1)+2$, which always leaves remainder $2$ on division by $4$. Example: $1+2+3+4=10$. A is false.
options: (i) Both A and R are true, and R explains A.
(ii) Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A.
(iii) A is true, but R is false.
(iv) A is false, but R is true.

sections.title: Section F · Digits in disguise
sections.note: Each letter stands for a digit. Different letters are different digits.

questions.text: $AB$ is a two-digit number with digits $A$ and $B$. $AB+BA=132$ and $A-B=2$. Find $AB$.
steps: We also know $A-B=2$. Add the two equations: $2A=14$, so $A=7$. Then $B=5$.

questions.text: Solve $\begin{array}{r}1A\\\times\ \ A\\\hline 9A\end{array}$, where $A$ is a digit.
steps: Units: $A\times A$ must end in $A$. Try the digits: $0\times0=0$, $1\times1=1$, $5\times5=25$, $6\times6=36$. So $A$ is $0, 1, 5$ or $6$.
Now the whole product must be $90+A$: $10\times0=0$, $11\times1=11$, $15\times5=75$, $16\times6=96$.
Only $16\times6=96$ works.

questions.text: Find the digits: $\begin{array}{r}A\,B\\+\,B\,A\\\hline 1\,6\,5\end{array}$ with $A>B$. How many answers are there?
steps: Pairs of different digits with sum $15$ and $A>B$: $(9,6)$ and $(8,7)$.
